questions.title: PostgreSQL vs MySQL — Key Differences
questions.question: What are the key differences between PostgreSQL and MySQL, and why would you choose PostgreSQL for a Java backend?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- PostgreSQL: object-relational, true SQL standard compliance, stronger ACID guarantees
- MySQL: faster simple reads historically, simpler setup, wider shared hosting availability
- PostgreSQL advantages: advanced data types (JSONB, arrays, ranges, enums), window functions, CTEs, full-text search, PostGIS
- PostgreSQL MVCC: readers never block writers; MySQL InnoDB also has MVCC but behaves differently
- PostgreSQL uses serializable snapshot isolation; MySQL relies more on lock-based approaches
- For complex queries, analytics, and JSON workloads: PostgreSQL is generally superior

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
PostgreSQL is an object-relational database that strictly follows the SQL standard and has a much richer feature set. For a Java backend, it's generally the better choice because of its support for complex data types like JSONB for flexible schema columns, arrays, range types, and powerful features like window functions, recursive CTEs, and full-text search — all built in without plugins.

MySQL historically had faster simple read performance and is simpler to set up, which made it popular for web applications in the early 2000s. But for the kind of analytical and complex transactional queries a Java backend typically runs, PostgreSQL's query planner and execution engine are generally superior.

PostgreSQL's MVCC implementation means readers never block writers and writers never block readers. A long-running report query won't hold up inserts. This is crucial for a backend that needs to handle concurrent reads and writes without one type of operation starving the other.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Feature Comparison

| Feature | PostgreSQL | MySQL |
|---------|-----------|-------|
| SQL compliance | Excellent | Partial |
| JSONB support | Native, indexed | JSON type, limited |
| Window functions | Full support | Basic support |
| Full-text search | Built-in | Via MyISAM or plugin |
| Array types | Native | Not supported |
| Range types | Native | Not supported |
| Partitioning | Declarative (PG10+) | Available |
| Materialized views | Supported | Not natively |
| Custom types/functions | Extensive | Limited |

## Spring Boot Configuration

```yaml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/appdb
    driver-class-name: org.postgresql.Driver
  jpa:
    database-platform: org.hibernate.dialect.PostgreSQLDialect
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate  # use Flyway/Liquibase for migrations
```

```xml
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.postgresql</groupId>
    <artifactId>postgresql</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
</dependency>
```

speakable_v2.cap: This is crucial for a backend that needs to handle concurrent reads and writes without one type of operation starving the other.

questions.title: PostgreSQL Data Types for Java Backends
questions.question: What are the most useful PostgreSQL data types for a Java backend that you should know?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- BIGINT for IDs (auto-increment with SERIAL/BIGSERIAL or IDENTITY)
- NUMERIC/DECIMAL for money — never use FLOAT for currency
- TIMESTAMPTZ stores time with timezone reference (use this over TIMESTAMP)
- VARCHAR vs TEXT: in PostgreSQL TEXT is not slower, length-constrained VARCHAR only matters for validation
- UUID: natively supported, good for distributed IDs
- JSONB: binary JSON with indexing support — vs JSON which just validates and stores text
- ENUM types: more readable than string, enforced by DB but costly to ALTER
- Arrays: store multiple values without a join table

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The data type choices that matter most in practice are around time, money, and flexible schema. For timestamps, always use TIMESTAMPTZ — timestamp with time zone — not plain TIMESTAMP. TIMESTAMPTZ stores everything in UTC and converts to the session timezone on display, which avoids an entire class of timezone bugs in distributed systems.

For monetary values, use NUMERIC or DECIMAL with explicit precision and scale — never a floating point type. Floats cannot represent many decimal values exactly, which leads to rounding errors in financial calculations. NUMERIC is exact.

JSONB is one of PostgreSQL's killer features. Unlike JSON which just validates and stores text as-is, JSONB parses the JSON into a binary format, stores it efficiently, and supports GIN indexing so you can query inside JSON documents with indexes. This gives you flexible schema storage without giving up the ability to search efficiently.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Essential Data Types

```sql
CREATE TABLE products (
    id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,           -- auto-increment 64-bit int
    public_id   UUID DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),  -- URL-safe public identifier
    name        TEXT NOT NULL,                   -- no length limit, same perf as VARCHAR
    sku         VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE,              -- VARCHAR when you want DB-level length validation
    price       NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL,         -- exact decimal — always for money
    stock       INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
    tags        TEXT[],                          -- array of strings
    metadata    JSONB,                           -- binary JSON with index support
    status      product_status NOT NULL,         -- enum type
    created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),       -- with timezone: stores UTC, shows local
    updated_at  TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- Create enum type first
CREATE TYPE product_status AS ENUM ('draft', 'active', 'discontinued');
```

## TIMESTAMPTZ vs TIMESTAMP

```sql
-- TIMESTAMP: stores exactly what you give it — timezone agnostic (dangerous)
INSERT INTO events (ts) VALUES ('2024-01-01 10:00:00');  -- which timezone? unknown!

-- TIMESTAMPTZ: normalizes to UTC, renders in session timezone
SET timezone = 'America/New_York';
INSERT INTO events (tstz) VALUES (NOW());  -- stored as UTC
SELECT tstz FROM events;  -- displayed in New York time

SET timezone = 'Asia/Kolkata';
SELECT tstz FROM events;  -- same moment, displayed in IST
```

## Array Type — Avoid a Join Table

```sql
-- Tags without a join table
INSERT INTO articles (title, tags)
VALUES ('Java Tips', ARRAY['java', 'backend', 'jpa']);

-- Query articles with any of these tags
SELECT title FROM articles
WHERE tags && ARRAY['java', 'spring'];  -- && = overlap (any match)

-- Query articles with ALL these tags
WHERE tags @> ARRAY['java', 'backend'];  -- @> = contains all

-- Index for fast array queries
CREATE INDEX idx_article_tags ON articles USING GIN (tags);
```

## Java Type Mappings

| PostgreSQL | Java |
|------------|------|
| BIGINT | Long |
| NUMERIC | BigDecimal |
| BOOLEAN | Boolean |
| TEXT/VARCHAR | String |
| TIMESTAMPTZ | OffsetDateTime / Instant |
| UUID | java.util.UUID |
| JSONB | String / custom type |
| TEXT[] | String[] |

speakable_v2.hook: The data type choices that matter most in practice are around time, money, and flexible schema.
speakable_v2.cap: This gives you flexible schema storage without giving up the ability to search efficiently.

questions.title: MVCC — How PostgreSQL Handles Concurrency
questions.question: How does PostgreSQL's MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) work?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- MVCC: each transaction sees a snapshot of the DB at a point in time
- No read-write locking — readers don't block writers and vice versa
- How: each row version has xmin (created by tx) and xmax (deleted/updated by tx)
- A transaction only sees rows where xmin is committed and < its snapshot txid, and xmax is null or > its snapshot
- Dead tuples: old versions left behind after updates — VACUUM reclaims them
- Transaction ID wraparound: 32-bit txid, must VACUUM regularly to avoid wraparound catastrophe

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
MVCC works by keeping multiple versions of each row rather than locking rows for access. When you update a row, PostgreSQL doesn't overwrite the old data — it creates a new version of the row and marks the old version as deleted. Any transaction that started before your update still sees the old version. Any transaction that started after your update sees the new version.

This is what allows readers and writers to work concurrently without blocking each other. A long-running report query takes a snapshot at its start time and consistently sees that snapshot throughout its execution, even as other transactions are inserting and updating data in the same tables.

The cost of this approach is dead tuples — old row versions that are no longer visible to any active transaction. These accumulate continuously on a busy table and must be cleaned up by AUTOVACUUM. If AUTOVACUUM falls behind, tables and indexes bloat and performance degrades. This is why monitoring AUTOVACUUM behavior is an important PostgreSQL operational concern.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Row Versioning (Hidden Columns)

```sql
-- PostgreSQL stores hidden system columns per row
SELECT ctid, xmin, xmax, name, salary FROM employees WHERE id = 1;
-- ctid:  physical location (page, offset)
-- xmin:  transaction that created this row version
-- xmax:  transaction that deleted/updated this row (0 = current)

-- After UPDATE:
-- Old row: xmin=100, xmax=205 (marked dead by tx 205)
-- New row: xmin=205, xmax=0  (current version)
```

## Snapshot Visibility

```
Transaction A starts (snapshot: sees txids < 200)
Transaction B starts (snapshot: sees txids < 200)

Transaction C (txid=201) updates row 1 and commits

Transaction A: still sees old row 1 (201 > A's snapshot boundary)
Transaction B: still sees old row 1 (same snapshot boundary)

Transaction D starts (snapshot: sees txids < 205)
Transaction D: sees new row 1 (201 < 205, and txid 201 is committed)
```

## VACUUM and Dead Tuple Cleanup

```sql
-- Monitor dead tuple accumulation
SELECT relname, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup,
       last_autovacuum, last_analyze
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE n_dead_tup > 10000
ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC;

-- Manual vacuum when needed
VACUUM (VERBOSE, ANALYZE) orders;

-- Full vacuum — reclaims disk space (requires exclusive lock, use during maintenance)
VACUUM FULL orders;
```

## Transaction ID Wraparound Prevention

```sql
-- 32-bit txid: ~2 billion values before wraparound
-- If transactions wrap, old data becomes invisible → database protection shutdown

-- Monitor oldest transactions still in use
SELECT datname, age(datfrozenxid) AS txid_age
FROM pg_database
ORDER BY txid_age DESC;
-- Alert if age > 1.5 billion — VACUUM FREEZE needed

-- Emergency freeze to prevent wraparound
VACUUM FREEZE table_name;
```

speakable_v2.hook: MVCC works by keeping multiple versions of each row rather than locking rows for access.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: This is why monitoring AUTOVACUUM behavior is an important PostgreSQL operational concern.

questions.title: Full-Text Search in PostgreSQL
questions.question: How does full-text search work in PostgreSQL and how do you implement it in a Java Spring application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- tsvector: document converted to searchable token list with positions
- tsquery: search query with operators: & (AND), | (OR), ! (NOT), <-> (phrase)
- GIN index on tsvector column for fast full-text search
- ts_rank() for relevance scoring and ordering results by relevance
- to_tsvector(language, text) and to_tsquery(language, query)
- Stored generated column for tsvector to avoid recomputing on every search
- Alternative: Elasticsearch for very large-scale or advanced search needs

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
PostgreSQL has built-in full-text search that's good enough for many applications without needing an external search engine. It works by converting text into a tsvector — a list of lexemes, which are normalized word stems with their positions in the document. Searching converts the query into a tsquery and matches it against the tsvector.

The practical advantage over LIKE queries is that tsvector handles stemming — searching for 'run' also finds 'running' and 'runs'. It handles stop words like 'the' and 'a' which would produce too many results to be useful. And with a GIN index, full-text search is much faster than a LIKE '%keyword%' query which requires a full table scan.

For a Spring application, the typical setup is to add a generated tsvector column to your table that automatically updates whenever the source text columns change, index it with GIN, and query it using native SQL since JPA doesn't have first-class full-text support.

questions.title: PostgreSQL Schemas, Roles and Security
questions.question: How do PostgreSQL schemas and roles work, and how do you set up proper security for a Java application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Schema: namespace within a database — like a folder for tables
- Default schema: 'public' — best practice: create app-specific schema
- Role: user or group in PostgreSQL — roles can own objects and have granted privileges
- Principle of least privilege: app role should only have SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on needed tables, not DDL
- GRANT/REVOKE: control access at table, schema, or database level
- Row-level security (RLS): filter rows based on who's querying — multi-tenant enforcement
- search_path: controls which schema PostgreSQL looks in first

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A schema in PostgreSQL is a namespace — a logical grouping of tables, views, and functions within a database. You can have multiple schemas in one database, which is useful for organizing objects or for multi-tenant setups where each tenant has their own schema.

Roles are PostgreSQL's unified concept for users and groups. You create a role, grant it specific privileges, and your application connects as that role. The key principle is least privilege — your application role should only have the permissions it actually needs: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE on specific tables. It should not have CREATE TABLE or DROP permissions, which prevents a SQL injection attack from being able to modify the schema.

Row-level security is a powerful feature for multi-tenant applications. You attach a policy to a table that filters which rows each role can see. The application sets a session variable for the current tenant ID, and the policy automatically restricts all queries to that tenant's rows without any application-level filtering code.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: A schema in PostgreSQL is a namespace — a logical grouping of tables, views, and functions within a database.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: The application sets a session variable for the current tenant ID, and the policy automatically restricts all queries to that tenant's rows without any application-level filtering code.

questions.title: JSONB — Flexible Schema in PostgreSQL
questions.question: How do you use JSONB in PostgreSQL for flexible schema storage and how do you query and index it?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- JSONB: binary JSON — parsed, de-duplicated keys, reordered — supports indexing
- JSON: plain text storage — preserves whitespace and key order — no indexing
- Operators: -> returns JSON, ->> returns text; #> and #>> for nested paths
- GIN index: index all keys in JSONB — fast for @> (containment) queries
- Expression index: index a specific JSONB key — faster for known key queries
- jsonb_set() to update specific keys without replacing entire object
- Pattern: use structured columns for queried fields, JSONB for flexible/optional metadata

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
JSONB is PostgreSQL's binary JSON column type. Unlike the JSON type which just validates and stores text as-is, JSONB parses the JSON into an internal binary format, removes duplicate keys, and normalizes whitespace. The benefit is that JSONB supports GIN indexing — you can create an index that covers all keys in the JSON document, enabling fast containment queries.

The choice between JSONB and structured columns is a design decision. A good rule of thumb: if you always need to query or filter on a field, make it a real column with an index. If it's variable metadata that you store and retrieve but don't typically filter by, JSONB is a good fit — it avoids schema migrations every time you add a new metadata field.

Updating specific keys in JSONB without replacing the entire document uses the jsonb_set function. This is important for efficiency and to avoid race conditions — replacing the entire JSON object in an UPDATE would lose concurrent changes to other keys in the same document.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: JSONB is PostgreSQL's binary JSON column type.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: This is important for efficiency and to avoid race conditions — replacing the entire JSON object in an UPDATE would lose concurrent changes to other keys in the same document.

questions.title: Database Migrations with Flyway
questions.question: How do you manage PostgreSQL schema migrations with Flyway in a Spring Boot application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Flyway: versioned SQL migration files applied in order, tracked in flyway_schema_history table
- Naming convention: V{version}__{description}.sql (two underscores)
- Never modify applied migrations — Flyway checksums prevent this from silently succeeding
- Repeatable migrations (R__): re-applied whenever their checksum changes (views, functions)
- Baseline: for existing databases, establish a baseline so Flyway knows where to start
- Rollback: Flyway OSS doesn't support SQL rollback scripts — design migrations as forward-only
- Spring Boot auto-runs migrations on startup before JPA initialization

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Flyway is a database migration tool that tracks which SQL scripts have been applied to your database using a history table. You write versioned SQL files that Flyway applies in version order. On application startup, Flyway checks which versions have already been applied and runs only the new ones. This makes deployments repeatable and auditable.

The golden rule with Flyway is to never modify a migration that has already been applied to any environment. Flyway stores a checksum for each migration and will refuse to start if a checksum doesn't match, protecting you from silently corrupting a database that already applied a different version of a script.

For production deployments, write migrations that are safe to run while the application is up — avoid long-running DDL that locks tables. Adding a new column is fast. Adding a NOT NULL column to a large table without a default requires a table rewrite, which can take minutes and block all writes. The safe pattern is to add the column as nullable first, backfill existing rows, then add the constraint separately.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Project Setup

```xml
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.flywaydb</groupId>
    <artifactId>flyway-core</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.flywaydb</groupId>
    <artifactId>flyway-database-postgresql</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  flyway:
    enabled: true
    locations: classpath:db/migration
    baseline-on-migrate: false  # true only for existing databases
```

## Migration File Examples

```
src/main/resources/db/migration/
├── V001__create_users_table.sql
├── V002__create_products_table.sql
├── V003__add_search_vector_to_products.sql
├── V004__create_orders_tables.sql
└── R__views_and_functions.sql  (repeatable — updates every time file changes)
```

```sql
-- V001__create_users_table.sql
CREATE TABLE app.users (
    id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    email       VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    name        TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON app.users (email);
```

```sql
-- V003__add_search_vector_to_products.sql
-- Safe zero-downtime migration: add nullable column, then add constraint
ALTER TABLE app.products
    ADD COLUMN search_vector TSVECTOR
    GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
        to_tsvector('english', coalesce(name, ''))
    ) STORED;

CREATE INDEX idx_products_fts ON app.products USING GIN (search_vector);
-- CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY won't work in a transaction;
-- use a separate repeatable script or manual step
```

## Zero-Downtime: Add NOT NULL Column Safely

```sql
-- V005__add_status_to_orders.sql
-- Step 1: Add nullable with default (fast)
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN status VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'pending';

-- Step 2: Backfill existing rows (run in small batches if table is huge)
UPDATE orders SET status = 'completed'
WHERE status IS NULL AND total_amount IS NOT NULL;

-- Step 3: Add NOT NULL constraint (fast if all rows filled)
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN status SET NOT NULL;
```

speakable_v2.hook: Flyway is a database migration tool that tracks which SQL scripts have been applied to your database using a history table.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: The safe pattern is to add the column as nullable first, backfill existing rows, then add the constraint separately.

questions.title: PostgreSQL Performance Monitoring
questions.question: What are the key PostgreSQL system views and tools you use to monitor and troubleshoot performance?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- pg_stat_activity: currently running queries, wait events, connection states
- pg_stat_user_tables: seq scans vs index scans, dead tuples, autovacuum timing
- pg_stat_user_indexes: which indexes are used (scans count)
- pg_stat_statements: aggregate query performance (total time, calls, mean, stddev)
- pg_locks: active locks and waiting queries
- EXPLAIN ANALYZE: query execution plan with actual stats
- log_min_duration_statement: capture slow queries in PostgreSQL logs

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
PostgreSQL exposes rich monitoring data through system views. The ones I check most often are pg_stat_activity for live query monitoring, pg_stat_statements for aggregate query performance analysis, and pg_stat_user_tables for understanding table health — particularly dead tuple accumulation and whether autovacuum is keeping up.

pg_stat_user_indexes is valuable for finding unused indexes. Any index that has zero or near-zero scans since the server last restarted is wasted overhead — it's slowing down writes without helping any queries. Dropping unused indexes is often an easy win for write-heavy tables.

For active incidents, pg_stat_activity combined with pg_locks lets you see which queries are waiting for locks and which queries are holding them. This is the first tool to reach for when the application suddenly slows and you suspect lock contention rather than a missing index.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Live Query Monitor

```sql
-- All active queries with duration
SELECT pid, usename, state,
       ROUND(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (NOW() - query_start))::NUMERIC, 1) AS seconds,
       wait_event_type, wait_event,
       LEFT(query, 100) AS query_preview
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state != 'idle'
  AND query NOT LIKE '%pg_stat_activity%'
ORDER BY seconds DESC NULLS LAST;
```

## Table Health Dashboard

```sql
SELECT relname,
       seq_scan,
       idx_scan,
       ROUND(100.0 * seq_scan / NULLIF(seq_scan + idx_scan, 0), 1) AS seq_pct,
       n_live_tup,
       n_dead_tup,
       ROUND(100.0 * n_dead_tup / NULLIF(n_live_tup + n_dead_tup, 0), 1) AS dead_pct,
       last_autovacuum
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC;

-- Alert: seq_pct > 50% on large tables = missing index
-- Alert: dead_pct > 10% = autovacuum not keeping up
```

## Top Slow Queries (pg_stat_statements)

```sql
SELECT LEFT(query, 80) AS query,
       calls,
       total_exec_time::INT AS total_ms,
       mean_exec_time::INT  AS avg_ms,
       stddev_exec_time::INT AS stddev_ms
FROM pg_stat_statements
WHERE calls > 10
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 15;
```

## Lock Contention Check

```sql
SELECT
    blocked.pid         AS waiting_pid,
    blocked.query       AS waiting_query,
    blocking.pid        AS blocking_pid,
    blocking.query      AS blocking_query,
    NOW() - blocked.query_start AS waiting_duration
FROM pg_stat_activity blocked
JOIN pg_stat_activity blocking
    ON blocking.pid = ANY(pg_blocking_pids(blocked.pid))
WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(blocked.pid)) > 0;
```

speakable_v2.hook: PostgreSQL exposes rich monitoring data through system views.
speakable_v2.cap: This is the first tool to reach for when the application suddenly slows and you suspect lock contention rather than a missing index.
